content: Peroxidases represent a large family of enzymes. The majority of peroxidase protein sequences are cataloged in the PeroxiBase database. These enzymes typically catalyze reactions involving the reduction of peroxides. For many peroxidases, hydrogen peroxide serves as the optimal substrate, although some exhibit greater activity with organic hydroperoxides, such as lipid peroxides. Peroxidases may contain a heme cofactor at their active sites or possess redox-active cysteine or selenocysteine residues. The specific nature of the electron donor is highly dependent on the structural characteristics of the enzyme. For instance, horseradish peroxidase can utilize a wide range of organic compounds as electron donors and acceptors. This is facilitated by its accessible active site, which allows many compounds to reach the reaction site. In contrast, cytochrome c peroxidase has a highly restricted active site, resulting in a much more specific selection of electron-donating compounds. Although the precise mechanisms of action remain to be fully elucidated, peroxidases are known to contribute to enhancing a plant's defense mechanisms against pathogens. Additionally, peroxidases are sometimes employed as histological markers in research and diagnostic applications. Cytochrome c peroxidase serves as a soluble and easily purified model for studying cytochrome c oxidase. Glutathione peroxidase, a peroxidase found in humans, contains selenocysteine and utilizes glutathione as an electron donor. This enzyme is active with both hydrogen peroxide and organic hydroperoxide substrates. Furthermore, amyloid beta, when bound to heme, has been demonstrated to exhibit peroxidase activity.
